1.why: The token is verified only against the hash of the recovery owned by the caller's session — ownedRecovery() rejects any recovery whose sessionId does not match the current session.

2.why: False: each session gets its own recovery with a distinct tokenHash, so a reset code issued to one session cannot validate against another session's recovery.

3.why: True: there is no session-invalidation logic after reset-password — the same session proceeds to privacy/confirmation and any other sessions remain valid.

4.why: The server only listens over TLS with cert/key and sets HSTS, but the TLS version is not explicitly pinned and relies on Bun defaults.

5.why: Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes and passwords as bcrypt (cost 12) — protected with appropriate one-way algorithms, though technically hashed rather than encrypted.

6.why: Responses are generic and contain no account data, but the simulated delivery exposes the recovery token itself in the page and browser console/logs.

7.why: Email, token, MFA code, password and cookie values are all validated with strict regexes/length caps, bodies are size-limited, and all DOM insertion uses textContent.

8.why: Navigation uses only whitelisted hash routes (safeHashView), no external redirects exist, and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none'.

9.why: No user input is ever rendered as HTML or script — dynamic values go through textContent and a nonce-based CSP blocks inline/untrusted scripts.

10.why: Error pages are generic with no stack traces, but the token is explicitly written to the on-page log panel and console ('Test reset token: ...'), so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and never stored, but the MFA secret code is hardcoded in the source as const MFA_CODE = "246810".

12.why: No default account credentials exist (there is no login at all), but the static, hardcoded, UI-displayed MFA code effectively functions as a well-known default credential.

13.why: Wrong attempts are throttled via per-recovery counters (5 attempts then a 60-second block) plus independent IP-based rate limits of 8 attempts per minute.

14.why: The /api/recovery response is deliberately identical regardless of email validity or account existence, and the UI states this explicitly.

15.why: The reset token is a 256-bit CSPRNG hex value bound to the session's recovery, but 'user-specific' holds only at session granularity since no user accounts exist.
